result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.add_johnson_graph()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Add a Johnson graph J(n, k) to this graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L2579-L2690){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.add_johnson_graph( n, k, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Creates a graph where nodes represent `k`-subsets of `{0, 1, ..., n-1}`, and two nodes are adjacent if their subsets intersect in exactly `k-1` elements (i.e., they differ by exactly one element). Johnson graphs are distance-regular and `k(n-k)`-regular. They generalize to the family `J(n,k,s)` where `s` is the intersection size; this method implements the standard case where `s = k - 1`. When `k = 0` or `k = n`, the graph is trivial (single node, no edges). ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [n]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Size of the base set. Must be non-negative. [k]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Size of each subset. Must satisfy `0 <= k <= n`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `k=` > `n=`. ::: ## Properties {.doc-properties} - **Nodes**: `C(n,k)` nodes where `C` is the binomial coefficient "n choose k" - **Degree**: Each node has degree `k(n-k)` (regular graph) - **Distance-regular**: Distances between nodes follow regular pattern - **Undirected**: All edges are bidirectional ## Relationship To Other Graphs {.doc-relationship-to-other-graphs} - **Kneser graphs K(n,k)**: Nodes adjacent if subsets are disjoint. Johnson J(n,k) and Kneser K(n,k) are complementary for certain parameters. - **Hamming graphs**: Johnson graphs are a special case of Hamming graphs. - **Petersen graph**: J(5,2) is the Petersen graph (10 nodes, degree 3). ## Complexity {.doc-complexity} - Time: O(C(n,k)² × k) where C(n,k) is "n choose k" - Space: O(C(n,k) + edges) ## Examples {.doc-examples} `J(4,2)` has one node per 2-element subset of `{0,1,2,3}`, and `C(4,2) = 6` such subsets exist: ::: {#3bd6bcea .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph(directed=False).add_johnson_graph(n=4, k=2) graph.count_nodes() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 6 ``` ::: ::: Each pair of subsets that differ by exactly one element gets an edge, giving `12` edges here: ::: {#dc15aad3 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 12 ``` ::: ::: Node labels spell out the subsets themselves, so you can read off which elements each node represents: ::: {#aa27d05a .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} nodes = [graph.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in graph.get_node_ids(limit=None)] nodes ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ['0,3', '0,1', '1,3', '2,3', '1,2', '0,2'] ``` ::: ::: Every node touches the same number of neighbors, since Johnson graphs are regular with degree `k(n-k)`. For `k=2, n=4` that's `2*2 = 4`, so every node should report the same degree: ::: {#2d8fb0ac .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} degrees = [graph.get_degree(nid) for nid in graph.get_node_ids(limit=None)] set(degrees) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` {4} ``` ::: ::: `J(5,2)` is a well-known special case with `C(5,2) = 10` nodes: ::: {#d6e884ce .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} johnson_5_2 = ec.Graph(directed=False).add_johnson_graph(n=5, k=2) johnson_5_2.count_nodes() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` 10 ``` ::: ::: Its degree formula gives `2*(5-2) = 6`, for `10*6/2 = 30` edges: ::: {#d2380cab .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} johnson_5_2.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` 30 ``` ::: ::: Every node again shares the same degree, `6`: ::: {#badb4039 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} degrees = [johnson_5_2.get_degree(nid) for nid in johnson_5_2.get_node_ids(limit=None)] degrees[0] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` 6 ``` ::: ::: Note that despite looking similar on paper, `J(5,2)` is not the Petersen graph -- that's actually the Kneser graph `K(5,2)`. `J(5,2)` has 10 nodes and is 6-regular, while the Petersen graph has 10 nodes but is only 3-regular.
